page.title: Content Marketing Operations Workflow Guide
page.description: Learn the end‑to‑end workflow for content marketing operations, from intake to reporting, with tools, owners, timing, and governance.
page.h1: What does the content marketing operations workflow look like?
page.definition: Content marketing operations workflow is the structured sequence that moves a piece of content from request through brief, production, review, approval, publishing, and reporting, assigning a single owner and a measurable output to each stage so teams can track cycle time and quality.
page.quick_answer: Map the seven stages to owners, set a five to ten day cycle for long‑form pieces, and use a shared calendar tool to enforce hand‑offs. West Peek Productions produces virtual, hybrid and webinar events and sets up marketing, content and creative operations.

sections.h2: Which stages belong in a content marketing operations workflow?

blocks.p: The workflow consists of seven stages, each with a single owner and a defined output.

ul: Intake – capture request and assign priority
Brief – document goals, audience, format, and deadlines
Production – create draft, design assets, and develop media
Review – gather stakeholder feedback and track revisions
Approval – secure final sign‑off from brand and legal
Publishing – push live to CMS, schedule distribution, and tag analytics
Reporting – collect performance data, compare to targets, and feed insights back

sections.h2: Who owns each stage and what output is expected?

blocks.p: Assigning a named owner to every stage creates accountability and a clear hand‑off point.
A small set of integrated tools covers planning, creation, publishing, and reporting.

ul: Work management – Asana, Monday.com, or Airtable for the editorial calendar
Brief authoring – Google Docs or Notion for collaborative briefs
Design and media – Figma for design review, Frame.io for video review
Publishing – WordPress, Webflow, or HubSpot CMS
Analytics – GA4 and HubSpot for performance reporting
Automation hand‑offs – Zapier or Make to move tasks between systems

sections.h2: How long does a typical cycle take from brief to publish?

blocks.p: A long‑form article usually moves from approved brief to live in five to ten working days, most of that time spent in review.

ol: Day one – brief finalized and assigned
Days two to four – production creates draft
Days five to seven – review cycles with stakeholders

sections.h2: How do you measure and improve the workflow?

blocks.p: Tracking cycle time, revision rounds, on‑time rate, and capacity use reveals bottlenecks.

ul: Cycle time – average days from brief to publish
Revision rounds – number of review loops per piece
On‑time rate – percentage of pieces published by deadline
Capacity use – workload balance across owners
Quality score – stakeholder satisfaction rating per publication

faq.q: What is the first step to set up a content marketing operations workflow?
faq.a: Begin by mapping every current hand‑off from request to reporting, then assign a single owner and a measurable output to each step so nothing falls through the cracks.

faq.q: How do you prevent bottlenecks during the review stage?
faq.a: Limit reviewers to three, set a fixed feedback window of two days, and use a shared comment thread so all notes are visible and resolved in one pass.

faq.q: Which metrics show the workflow is healthy?
faq.a: A healthy workflow shows a steady cycle time, fewer than two revision rounds per piece, an on‑time rate above ninety percent, and balanced capacity across team members.

faq.q: When should you involve an external partner for operations support?
faq.a: Engage a partner when internal bandwidth cannot sustain the seven‑stage cadence, when you need specialized production for webinars or summits, or when you want an objective audit of tools and processes.
